The less prominent phenotypic consequences of Klinefelter's syndrome (47, XXY) compared to Down's syndrome (trisomy 21) are due to dosage compensation via X-inactivation. In individuals with extra X chromosomes, all but one X chromosome are transcriptionally silenced in a process that involves chromatin methylation by histone methyltransferases (and other epigenetic modifications) during early embryonic development. This prevents overexpression of X-linked genes. In contrast, trisomy 21 lacks such a compensatory mechanism, leading to more severe phenotypic effects from gene dosage imbalance.
